items.title: 4 bodies found as search continues for climbers missing after Broad Peak avalanche
items.description: GILGIT: Four bodies were found on Friday as a search operation was underway to locate climbers who went missing on Broad Peak a day earlier after an avalanche struck around midday. The Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) said that the 10-member team included six Nepalese climbers, a Pakistani, an Omani, an American and a climber from China. The climbers from Nepal were identified as renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja, Pur Bahadur Gurung, Kili Pemba Sherpa, Nima Sherpa, Nawang Thindu Sherpa and Gyalu Sherpa. It identified the remaining climbers as Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman, Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi, Wang Zhong from China and Mallory Geis from the United States. ACP President Major General Irfan Arshad told Dawn on Friday that four bodies had been found. He identified two of the dead as Oman’s Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy and Nepal’s Pur Bahadur Gurung. Rescue operation In a statement issued earlier in the day, ACP Senior Vice President Karrar Haidri said two Pakistan Army Aviation rescue helicopters, carrying rescue personnel and additional specialised equipment, had been dispatched to support the ongoing search and rescue operation. The statement said the ACP president, along with the club’s senior leadership, remained in constant contact with the highest government authorities and relevant agencies to facilitate the rescue operation. “Every possible effort is being made to ensure that helicopter support and all available rescue resources are mobilised at the earliest opportunity, subject to weather and operational conditions,” it added. The club said it was closely monitoring the situation and coordinating with all relevant stakeholders while expressing solidarity with the climbers’ families and the international mountaineering community. ACP’s General Secretary Ayaz Shigri told Dawn that several expedition teams had jointly begun their summit push before the incident. He said GPS locations received from some of the missing climbers indicated that the avalanche had swept the group about 1,000 metres downhill, leaving them trapped. Shigri said helicopter-assisted rescue operations were expected to begin on Friday morning. He said there were also fears that some local high-altitude porters might have been affected by the avalanche. “We pray for the safety of all the climbers. It is a big incident,” he said. Meanwhile, Gilgit-Baltistan Chief Minister Amjad Hussain Advocate directed all relevant departments to remain on high alert and expedite the search and rescue operation in coordination with the Pakistan Army, according to an official statement. He instructed the district administration and concerned authorities to utilise all available resources to ensure the climbers’ safety. Gilgit-Baltistan Minister for Tourism, Sports and Culture Naiknam Karim also expressed sorrow over the incident and said the provincial government was making every possible effort to locate and safely rescue the missing climbers. In a statement, he said “all relevant departments are in constant coordination and that every available resource was being utilised to support the ongoing search and rescue operation”. Expressing hope that the missing climbers would be found safe, the minister directed the concerned authorities to further expedite the rescue operation and ensure that all necessary logistical and operational support was provided to the teams working in the field. Purja, 43, who served with Britain’s Brigade of Gurkhas before joining the Special Boat Squadron of the Royal Marines, has broken multiple climbing records since becoming a full-time mountaineer and tour guide. He climbed all 14 “eight-thousanders” (peaks above 8,000 metres, or 26,000 feet) in six months and six days between April and October 2019 — then a record. In 2021, Purja completed the first winter ascent of K2 along with a team of nine other Nepalese climbers. Separately, in a post on X, the UK Embassy in Pakistan expressed concern at the incident. Seemingly referencing Purja, it also took note of a British-Nepali national missing in the expedition. “We are concerned by reports that several climbers have gone missing during a Broad Peak expedition, including a British-Nepali national,” the embassy said, adding that it remained in contact with Pakistani authorities. Sakhi, who hails from Hunza, had successfully summited Kanchenjunga (8,58­6m), the world’s 3rd highest mountain, in Nepal earlier in May. He had previously scaled K2, Nanga Parbat, Gasherbrum I and Gasherbrum II without supplemental oxygen, establishing himself among the country’s strongest high-altitude climbers. Additional input from AFP

items.title: Trump says deal reached for 'complete disarmament' of Hamas
items.description: US President Donald Trump said talks in Cairo between mediators and Hamas leaders on Thursday have led to a phased disarmament agreement in Gaza, but a Hamas official described the deal as a draft and US officials said Israel was sceptical the Palestinian group would surrender its weapons. “Today, the Board of Peace reached a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza,” Trump said in a social media post, adding that the disarmament would come in phases. “This is a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY.” The agreement was a critical step towards Gaza being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the so-called Board of Peace, Trump said. “At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks,” he added. The Israeli embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s announcement. A Hamas source told Reuters the “draft agreement” stipulates that heavy weapons would only be stored and kept under the control of a Palestinian administration, and the weapons cannot be transferred to Israel. “We will not take any action regarding disarmament prior to Israel’s withdrawal from the Strip,” Ghazi Hamad, a member of the Hamas negotiating team, told Al Jazeera . A US official on Thursday told reporters that Israel is “very sceptical that Hamas will disarm”. “We’re very confident they will adhere to it,” the US official added. “If they don’t, obviously President Trump would be very, very disappointed.” There were also questions about how long the process would take. A Board of Peace official gave an estimate of 200 to 320 days, but a US official played down that timeline. An Israeli official, who declined to be identified, said before Trump’s announcement Israel had rejected a proposal. “Israel demands the complete disarmament of Hamas, including the removal of weapons from Gaza and the complete demilitarisation of the Strip as a precondition for any process,” the official said earlier on Thursday. “The 15-point document in question does not provide a satisfactory response to these demands and Israel conveyed its objections.” Earlier, Israeli strikes killed at least six Palestinians in Gaza, including two children, medics said. A roadmap towards Hamas disarmament? Hamas leaders held talks with mediators from Egypt, Qatar and Turkiye on the second phase of Trump’s Gaza plan, as presented to them by his Board of Peace . Trump set up the board to oversee a plan to end Israel’s war in Gaza and rebuild the devastated territory. He appointed members of the board with himself as chair and said last year that the board will supervise Gaza’s temporary governance. “Ahead of us is a Gaza rebuilt, governed by Palestinians and at peace with Israel an a political horizon to a meaningful resolution the Israeli Palestinian conflict,” Nickolay Mladenov, Trump’s Board of Peace envoy for Gaza, said in a statement after the president’s post. Officials involved in the talks shared few details about plans to rebuild Gaza. The plan also calls for a surge in humanitarian aid, governance by a civilian Palestinian administration, the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza and the deployment of an international force to help maintain security. Handover of weapons could be sticking point The reality on the ground in Gaza, so far, remains far from the goals of the agreement. Hamas wants Israel to commit to ending attacks on Gaza and withdraw its forces. It is not yet clear what will happen regarding light or personal weapons or whether the new Hamas stance will be accepted by Israel or the Board of Peace. The plan includes the elimination of tunnels, arms stockpiles and weapons production facilities, a diplomat involved in the talks said. “This isn’t really a trust deal,” a US official said on Thursday, calling the agreement a “conditions-based deal.” The Israeli military has continued to expand its military occupation of Gaza, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu saying that Israel intends to expand the area under its control to 70pc of the enclave. It remains unclear how many forces would be available to deploy with the planned International Stabilisation Force , and whether Israeli troops would withdraw from the enclave. Israel will need to leave Gaza Strip: EU The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas has welcomed the agreement with Hamas, but notes that “a lot needs to fall into place” for the deal to work, and that Israel needs to withdraw from the Gaza Strip to enable verification practices. “The plan to disarm Hamas in Gaza, if fully implemented, would be a constructive step towards peace,” she writes on X. “Success depends on the full commitment of all parties. “Verifying Hamas’ compliance will be a significant challenge. Israel would need to eventually withdraw from Gaza,” Kallas adds. She says that the bloc stands ready to support the next steps, including the entry of the National Committee and International Stabilisation Force. Kallas adds that two EU missions on the ground will play an important role in supporting Palestinian state-building efforts. Attacks continue Health officials said separate Israeli strikes had killed at least two children, a woman and three men in Gaza on Thursday. The Israeli military said it struck Hamas fighters in the enclave. The ceasefire in Gaza has been repeatedly violated, with more than 1,200 Palestinians, mostly civilians, being killed by Israeli attacks and four Israeli soldiers being killed since the truce began in October, according to Gaza health officials and Israeli authorities, respectively.

items.title: Good governance 'quintessential' for security and stability of Pakistan: DG ISPR
items.description: Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General (DG) Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry termed good governance “quintessential” for the security and stability of Pakistan. He made this remark while addressing a press conference focused on the overall security situation in the country, particularly Balochistan. The DG ISPR, during his presser, commented on Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s remarks about the need for new administrative units in Pakistan: “We have been saying this earlier also as a primary stakeholder in security that good governance is essential for the security and stability of Pakistan.” Without this, he stressed that none of Pakistan’s issues could be resolved. He said that the National Action Plan (NAP), with its 14-point agenda and consensus of all political parties, depended on good governance for its implementation, adding, “good governance is quintessential for Pakistan”. “Now how to get the good governance? The politicians and political parties have to decide. If you ask us, yes, there has to be a serious discussion on it.” “Now our population is 240-250m people, and we still have four provinces. We have to see whether it is serving good governance? That debate has to be sensibly done by politicians, by those in power, even those who have been previously in power, and those who are responsible to the people of Pakistan,” the DG ISPR said, mentioning that it had to be done as per the will of the people of Pakistan. “The will of the people of Pakistan is superior. If good governance requires an administrative reset, then it has to be done. Through constitutional methods, legal methods, and through political representatives.” 10 terrorists killed per day in 2026 At the outset of the briefing, the military’s spokesperson said 40,348 intelligence-based operations had been conducted this year so far, adding that the figure covered operations carried out by all security forces, including police, civil armed forces, intelligence agencies and the armed forces. Of these operations, most were carried out in Balochistan, with the number exceeding 31,000, he said. The DG ISPR added that overall 3,145 terrorism incidents had taken place in the country in 2026, among which 1,971 were reported from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 1,148 from Balochistan and 26 from other parts of the country. During this time, he continued, 2,084 individuals who were confirmed terrorists were killed. “This comes to an average of 10 terrorists being killed every day, which is the highest ratio ever,” he added. Meanwhile, security forces were undertaking nearly 200 intelligence-based operations (IBO) per day. “So these IBOs are going on every hour.” The DG ISPR further stated that “819 Pakistanis have been martyred” in incidents of terrorism in the ongoing year, which came to four per day. This comprised 303 army personnel, 194 law enforcers from police and civil armed forces and 322 civilians. He added that 28 incidents of suicide bombing had taken place this year, “the majority of which were carried out by Afghan nationals […] and people associated with their security forces”. Comparing the number of terrorists killed last year with those killed in 2026, he said 2,597 were killed in 2025 and 2,084 this year so far. Pointing out that five months were left before 2026 would end, he said, “The way the kinetic prong of the counter-terrorism is maturing, responding and delivering, that is before you.” He further elaborated that the number of martyrs in comparison to slain terrorists was higher, but the tide started turning in 2024. And in 2025, “for each martyr we were taking out minimum two [terrorists], and this year, we are taking out minimum 2.5 [terrorists].” Here, he added, a valid question to ask would be why terrorism incidents are rising. “Because once returns from other elements of their strategy begin diminishing, they focus more here. And you saw when their direct strategy during Marka-i-Haq failed, they started investing a lot more here,” he explained. The DG ISPR added this also had to do with the “agenda of the terrorist-supporting Taliban regime” and the clarity that the state of Pakistan had. “These terrorists and their sponsors have come to understand that there is no space for appeasement or any talks with them […] They know that the state is telling them very clearly that either you submit to the state’s will in accordance with law and the Constitution, otherwise we are here and fighting,” he said. Moreover, he added, this also had to do with the proactive nature of the operations. “These [terrorism] incidents also rise because when we get proactive […] there will be more engagements.” ‘Hard state, question mark’ Speaking of the “perception that the situation in Balochistan has worsened”, he said this matter would be discerned by answering three questions. The first question was what the issue was, the second was what was happening and the third was what was being done, he said. Coming to the first question, he said the issue was not just specific to Balochistan but covered the overall security environment in Pakistan. The issue, he said, was “Hard state, question mark.” “Are we a hard state? Unfortunately not,” the military’s spokesperson added. Explaining the reason behind his answer, he said a hard state was one where the constitution and law were the same for everyone. “That is what a hard state is. It does not mean a military-run state, it does not mean an armed forces-dominated state,” he added. The DG ISPR said a state where all matters were decided in accordance with law and the constitution, where everyone was equal, was a hard state. And in that hard state, there would be security and stability; there would be no grievances. Then there was also the matter of obligations versus rights, he said, adding that it pertained to being aware of one’s responsibilities before speaking about one’s rights. “We are all taking up grievances — at some places slogans are also being raised in connection with those grievances and even arms are being taken up in some instances — and all those grievances [pertain to demand for rights],” he said. Saying that the demands for rights and grievances may be genuine, he added that obligations needed to be fulfilled first. “Let me try to explain the context constitutionally,” he said, quoting Article 5 of the Constitution. The provision preceded Article 8, which elaborated on fundamental rights, he said, adding that Article stated: “Loyalty to the state and obedience to the Constitution and law. It says loyalty to the state is the basic duty of every citizen. Full stop. Absolutely clear. “The provision’s second part states that obedience to the Constitution and law is the inviolable obligation of every citizen wherever he may be.” So the Constitution is “clear that we have some fundamental duties that we need to be loyal to the state”. “If we are loyal to the state and we are obedient to the Constitution and the law, then you can talk about your rights,” he said. Citing a statement by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir at the National Workshop in Balochistan recently, he said when the rights movement is talked about, why not an “obligations movement”. “There has to be a movement for the obligation of every citizen,” he asserted. Further speaking of the obligations, he said, “Is this not an obligation for every citizen that our first and final identity should be Pakistani? … We are citizens of this state, so our first identity and our last identity and the foremost identity is being a Pakistani. “It is our obligation to acknowledge the fundamental position, the central position of the state of Pakistan because if there is the state, there is politics, there is life […] These are our fundamental obligations. “Are we working towards that? Let’s think about it.” Focusing on Balochistan, he said the fundamental issue in the province was elitism and sardarism , and the desire to maintain the status quo. “This is that part of society that believes it has no obligations and only thinks of their rights. The elites, the sardars are a part of it. And I am not talking about all of them but those who believe that this status quo must be maintained,” the DG ISPR said. He added that this status quo predated 1947, under which a poor man’s child could not get education and progress. The people who did not want the status quo to change were the “prime movers of terrorism because they are afraid that the times are changing”. Then, there is the issue of the desire for appeasement, the DG ISPR said. “They do terrorism, they talk about terrorism and say that Balochistan is getting out of hand. Then they expect that we talk to them, appease them […] No, we will not. We will talk with the actual stakeholders, which are the people of Baluchistan,” he added. “You are not the stakeholder. You are only a stakeholder in your own personal and your family’s fortune.” The military’s spokesperson went on to say that the problem of such elements was that they were not being appeased. “They have this habit of thinking that Levies force is their private force, their sardari force.” “So once you start turning Balochistan’s Levies into a police force, they have a problem.” He further said that these elements were involved in smuggling in the name of business. “And if you stop this, there is terrorism. They promote terrorism and say Balochistan is getting out of hand. They demand that permits are issued, they get a share from the budget of more than Rs1,000 […] But no more.” Moving on, the DG ISPR said a third issue was “external power play”. The “elitists and sardarists have a common agenda”, he said, adding the “external powers” realise that Balochistan was blessed with not just “a very vibrant and very progressive human resource” but also with natural resources. “It has a blue economy, agriculture. They know the potential of Balochistan. They realise that when Balochistan rises, entire Pakistan rises and the region rises. And they have a problem, so they get physically involved through these terrorists […] and they find ready partners in these elitists and sardarists,” he said. Moreover, there was the issue of “contiguous support bases”, especially from Afghanistan. He said the business of the Afghan Taliban regime was terrorism and through terrorism, they sustained their economy, state and even diplomacy. “Even their diplomacy is centred on terrorism. What is common between India and Afghanistan, except their DNA? The only thing common is terrorism,” he added. “What is common between Fitna-al-Hindustan and Fitna-al-Khawarij ? Nothing. One is secular and nationalist, and the other is hardcore religious extremist. But because they are carrying out coordinated operations now,” he said. The government labelled the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan as Fitna-al-Khawarij and designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna-al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. He further stated that propaganda was another issue, which had three strands: a sense of deprivation, lack of representation and missing persons. Sharing data of facilities in various areas of Balochistan, he said the per capita budget of Balochistan was more than Rs75,000, which was more than any other province. “Then on what basis is this narrative of a sense of deprivation in Balochistan spun? It is spun on actions to prevent development. That is why they kill labourers and attack roads and hospitals and bridges. Are these military targets?” the DG ISPR questioned. Coming to the issue of lack of representation, he said same people and their families were in the assemblies since 1973. “Most of them are the same khanzaday and nawabzaday . It’s the same religious parties and same names, and either they win or their family members win. If they win, it is democracy, but if they don’t win, [the narrative is] there is dictatorship.” On missing persons, he said the government had formed a commission to inquire into the matter. The DG ISPR said the commission had received just 10,901 applications since its formation in the early 2010s. Of those, 9,372 cases had been disposed of, he said, adding that in 4,896 of the disposed-of cases, missing people had returned home, around 1,030 were located in prisons, 308 were found dead and 2,400 cases were declared as misreported cases. Moreover, he said, 2,933 of the total cases were reported from Balochistan, among which 2, 767 had been disposed of. He went on to say persons reported missing in the remaining cases were often found among killed terrorists after operations. The DG ISPR added that terrorists were now also filming attacks to build a narrative that the situation in Balochistan was deteriorating. He further pointed out that Balochistan’s area was 347,190 sq km, which was more than the area of many countries, as he elaborated on the need for more security personnel. He said this while speaking about raising a new command of the Frontier Corps, FC West, and its attached units in the province. Sharing details of the current situation in Balochistan, he said terrorists had killed 178 civilians in the province this year, kidnapped 55 civilians, damaged roads and bridges at 24 places, set property on fire at 60 places and there were 47 incidents of looting. Police and Levies were targeted in 105 incidents, he said. They carry out terrorist activities, film it and release videos, and “elitists and sardarists start crying over the deteriorating situation”, he added. They target infrastructure and run this propaganda about a lack of development, the military’s spokesperson said, mentioning Indian involvement in such activities as well. Here, he also spoke about challenges faced by police as first responders, again mentioning the vast area of Balochistan, in addition to capacity constraints. The DG ISPR further said that previous governments that let Levies be a “sardari force” were answerable in this regard. He questioned why the funds were not translated into equipment for police, adding, “Because you did not want to respond to your BLA pets.” He then lauded police for fighting against terrorism, asking why were they not being acknowledged. “Because terrorists are making videos […] that are used to create a narrative,” he answered. Moreover, he said, terrorists were “honey-trapping” girls. They would kidnap and abuse them and then blackmail them to commit acts of terrorism. He also said that 300 Indian websites were being operated for terrorism in Balochistan, more than 1,000 social media accounts were being used for the purpose and “hostile diaspora” was also involved in propaganda related to terrorism. Explaining the social media ecosystem in use of the terrorists, the DG ISPR said “First, an event or incident is seeded right or wrong and then it is framed by intiators, who then hand it over to amplifiers and then mass amplification is done by mainstream indian media, channels and their print media as well, from where it is picked up by international media and then you take it and run it as facts”. Citing the example of the July 16 attack on a convoy in Mastung, the military spokesperson said that accounts associated with BYC, BLA and political parties, operating from abroad, were involved in amplifying it. He further noted, “There is already an ecosystem here that whenever there is negative news about Pakistan, certain actors are always there to mark their attendance”. Speaking of kinetic operations against terrorists in Balochistan, he said currently security forces were conducting Operation Shaban, which had been morphed into Operation Al-Azm. He also said that most of the operations were carried out jointly by the army, FC and police. Moreover, Operation Ghazab lil-Haq was also under way against the Afghan Taliban. The military’s spokesperson said that 2.6m Afghan had been repatriated to Afghanistan from Pakistan, of whom 600,000 were repatriated this year. He also said that work was underway to strengthen the capacity of security forces in the province, including the establishment of FC West in Chaghi, which he said will ensure the “security of the mineral corridor”. The DG ISPR added that the government was working on the police force as well, with newly recruited ASPs being posted to Balochistan and provision of bulletproof vehicles among other measures. He also stressed the significance of “empowering and appeasing” the common people of Balochistan. “We are committed to engage and talk directly with people,” he said. He added that Rs70bn had been allocated to socioeconomic projects in Balochistan and Rs24bn for the Balochistan Special Development Initiative. He further stated that development projects aimed at improving road connectivity, IT training, and human resources were also in process. The DG ISPR, concluding his address, played a video of the government’s direct engagements within Balochistan. “This is the bright future of Balochistan that we need to further nurture, develop and propagate because Balochistan has a remarkable future,” he said. “In the words of the Field Marshal, and he says it with a lot of conviction, that within 5-10 years it is going to be the richest province; it is going to be a game changer. And the bigger the potential, the bigger the threats we face, but we, the people of Pakistan and Balochistan, will overcome (them).” ‘Kashmir jugular vein of Pakistan’ On the unrest in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), DG ISPR held, “Kashmir was, is and will remain a jugular vein of Pakistan.” “Only one voice is coming from Pakistan: Kashmir will be Pakistan, and there is only one voice coming from Kashmir: Pakistan is ours, we are Pakistani, nothing can change that.” Referring to the Joint Awami Action Committee’s (JAAC) protests, he said that “we knew who was behind that movement, but we wanted them to expose themselves. They have been exposed now”. He said that JAAC opposed refugee representation in AJK’s legislature; however, the state had asked them “wholeheartedly” to contest the elections and approach the matter legally and constitutionally. “However, they want to do this by force, but only the state has the monopoly of violence.” More to follow

items.title: After the floods comes super El Niño and potential droughts
items.description: Ghana is facing a double-edged climate risk in 2026: counting the cost of catastrophic floods while bracing for possible drought within the same rainy season. Barely a month ago, Ghana was reeling from devastating floods. On June 28–29, 2026, a violent rainstorm triggered flash floods across Greater Accra and parts of southern Ghana. Neighbourhoods including Spintex, Adabraka, Achimota, and Agbogbloshie went underwater, major arteries like the N1 were impassable, and homes, vehicles, and businesses were destroyed. Cape Coast, Kumasi and other cities in southern Ghana have also experienced flooding during this year’s rainy season. These floods have left dozens dead across the cities. Damage assessments put losses in the hundreds of millions of dollars, which is expected to increase once indirect costs to trade and small businesses are included; the government released GH¢300 million from its Contingency Fund for immediate response. It may seem paradoxical, but that same climate system now points toward the opposite hazard of dry spells and drought for the rest of the year. The intense rains of late June were consistent with a normal rainfall expected during the peak of the main rainy season in southern Ghana. For the rest of the year, Ghana will be dealing with a strengthening El Niño that historically tilts the odds toward below-normal rainfall and early-ending rains later in the season. A Strong El Niño Confirmed Earlier this year, we published this article showing that after nearly two years dominated by La Niña and neutral conditions, the tropical Pacific was tilting toward an El Niño event for late 2026 into 2027. At the time, the signal was still probabilistic. A cluster of international climate models was converging on a common signal for an El Niño event but the timing and eventual strength of the event remained uncertain. That caution has now given way to confirmation. In its Global Seasonal Climate Update, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed that El Niño conditions have developed in the tropical Pacific and are strengthening rapidly, with a strong El Niño event projected for July–September 2026. Multi-model ensembles from leading forecasting centres show a consistent and pronounced warming of sea-surface temperatures across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, with seasonal anomalies expected to exceed 2°C in key monitoring regions. The WMO first flagged the transition in June, giving an 80% probability of El Niño emerging between June and August 2026, rising to around 90% thereafter. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center went further, assigning a 63% chance the event reaches very strong intensity by November 2026–January 2027 (see Figure 1). The projected conditions are comparable to the historic 1997/98 and 2015/16 Super El Niños. Figure 1: Illustrative evolution of the Niño 3.4 sea-surface temperature anomaly through the 2026/27 event, based on WMO and NOAA CPC seasonal outlooks. Values are indicative of the forecast trajectory, not official real-time readings. What El Niño Does to the World’s Weather El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural, irregular cycle (roughly every two to seven years) driven by fluctuations in sea-surface temperature and atmospheric pressure across the tropical Pacific. During an El Niño event, the eastern and central Pacific warms well above average, weakening the trade winds that normally push warm surface water westward. This reorganises the pattern of rising and sinking air across the tropics, and changes rainfall patterns across the globe. Because the atmosphere is a single connected system, this Pacific disturbance has knock-on effects. These knock-on effects are referred to as teleconnections and have impacts on global rainfall and temperature patterns to varying degrees. Typically, El Niño brings wetter conditions to parts of South America, the southern United States, and East Africa. In Australia, Indonesia, southern Africa, and much of West Africa’s Gulf of Guinea coast, El Niño leads to drier conditions (see Figure 2). It also tends to raise global average temperatures, since the extra ocean heat adds to the atmosphere’s existing warming trend. This pattern has contributed to prior strong events becoming some of the hottest years on record. Figure 2: Schematic diagram of El Nino impacts on global rainfall showing areas which get wetter (green) and dryer (orange) as a result of the impact of El Nino events. Ghana’s El Niño Track Record Ghana’s rainfall is not immune to these Pacific-driven shifts, and the country’s climate record carries the scars of its three most significant El Niño events. The 1982/83 El Niño produced what remains Ghana’s most severe modern drought. Rainfall reduced across the country, and the resulting dry spell combined with widespread bushfires to destroy thousands of hectares of cocoa farms, damage food crops, and trigger localised famine. Station data from the period show the deficit was not simply low annual totals. Similarly, in 1997/98, there was another El Niño event, one of the strongest on record globally. This event similarly disrupted West African rainfall patterns, contributing to below-normal totals across parts of the Guinea Coast and reinforcing the region’s vulnerability to Pacific-driven dry spells. The 2015/16 event, comparable in strength to 1997/98, again brought drought stress to Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, the world’s two largest cocoa producers. Regional studies identify 2015/16, alongside 1982/83, as among the most severe drought periods recorded across Ghana’s cocoa agroforestry belt in the past four decades, with reduced rainfall and elevated temperatures pushing crop water stress to unusually high levels. Across all three episodes, the common thread is a weakened or shortened rainy season, disproportionately affecting the second half of the growing calendar — precisely when crops are most sensitive to moisture stress. What to Expect This Season Regional guidance issued in mid-2026 points to a similar, though not identical, pattern for the 2026/2027 El Niño event. Seasonal outlooks from AGRHYMET’s Regional Climate Centre and the WMO Coordination Mechanism, discussed at a June 2026 briefing for UN agencies and humanitarian partners, indicate a pronounced east–west contrast in rainfall probabilities across equatorial Africa, with below-normal rainfall favoured across large parts of the Sahel and mixed signals across the Gulf of Guinea. For Ghana specifically, the most consistent risk signal points to below-normal rainfall during the minor rainy season (roughly September–November) in southern Ghana , the period historically most sensitive to El Niño’s influence on the West African monsoon. In the north, where the rains follow a single unimodal season running from around May to October, forecasts point toward an earlier-than-normal cessation of rainfall , shortening the effective growing window (see Figure 3). Should this pattern hold, a weak minor season in the south combined with a truncated main season in the north raises a real risk of localised dry spells in the coming months. Figure 3: Illustration of the rainfall risk pattern associated with the 2026/27 El Niño. The blue lines show the expected rainfall patterns in Southern and Northern Ghana from previous records while the red bars are the expected rainfall due to the effect of El Niño. Why This Matters: Crops, Fires, and the Economy A rainfall deficit of this kind would arrive at a delicate moment for Ghana’s agriculture-dependent economy, with consequences likely to unfold across several fronts. Crop yields and food security: Cocoa, maize, and other rain-fed staples are highly sensitive to moisture stress during flowering and pod- or grain-filling stages. Ghana’s experience in 1982/83 and 2015/16 shows that shortened rains and elevated temperatures can sharply depress both yields and planted area, with knock-on effects for household food security and rural incomes. Bushfires: Drier vegetation and extended dry spells raise the likelihood and severity of bushfires, particularly in the transition and savanna zones and in cocoa farms where dried undergrowth and harvest residue provide ready fuel — a dynamic that contributed directly to farm losses in 1982/83. Economic ripple effects: As the world’s second-largest cocoa producer, a significant shortfall can hit export revenue, farmer incomes, and global cocoa prices at once. Reduced hydropower generation, strained irrigation supplies, and higher food prices are additional downstream risks to monitor. None of this is predetermined. El Niño shifts the odds toward drier conditions in these windows; it does not guarantee a specific outcome everywhere. But given Ghana’s documented sensitivity to past events of this strength, the coming minor season in the south and the tail end of the main season in the north deserve close monitoring by farmers, water managers, and disaster-preparedness agencies alike. Authors: Frederick Otu-Larbi ( frederick.otu-larbi@uenr.edu.gh ) Caleb Mensah ( caleb.mensah@uenr.edu.gh ) Affiliation: Department of Atmospheric and Climate Science, University of Energy and Natural Resources, UENR.

items.title: 27e Fête du trône: «Avec le Burkina Faso, nos relations bilatérales sont très excellentes»
items.description: Le Maroc et le Burkina Faso ont célébré, solennellement, leur coopération, à l'ambassade du Royaume chérifien à Ouagadougou, dans la soirée du jeudi 30 juillet 2026, à l'occasion du 27e anniversaire de l'accession du Roi Mohammed VI au Trône. «Avec le Burkina Faso, nos relations bilatérales sont très excellentes», a déclaré l’ambassadeur du Royaume du Maroc au Burkina Faso, Youssef Slaoui. L'ambassade du Royaume du Maroc au Burkina Faso, a commémoré, le jeudi 30 juillet 2026, à Ouagadougou, la 27e année de l'accession au Trône du Roi Mohammed VI. Les amis du Royaume chérifien dont des membres du gouvernement, des présidents d'institutions, des chefs de missions diplomatiques et consulaires, des Représentants des Organisations internationales et interafricaines, des opérateurs économiques, des leaders religieux, entre autres, ont répondu massivement présent à la cérémonie marquée par des allocutions, la coupure du gâteau d’anniversaire et la traditionnelle photo de famille pour immortaliser le rendez-vous. Le gâteau d'anniversaire des 27 ans d'accession du Roi du Maroc, Mohammed VI au Trône «Le Maroc est un moteur économique en pleine mutation. Il est devenu l'économie la plus industrialisée d'Afrique, selon le dernier rapport de la Banque Africaine de Développement (BAD). C'est le fruit d'une montée en gamme industrielle, de la diversification des exportations et d'une politique industrielle vigoureuse», a déclaré l’ambassadeur du Royaume du Maroc au Burkina Faso, Youssef Slaoui. Le diplomate marocain s’est réjoui car, fort de ces acquis, son pays se projette vers l'avenir avec optimisme, en orientant ses priorités vers un potentiel de transformation économique majeur, marquant l'avènement d'une nouvelle ère portée par des réformes audacieuses, des investissements stratégiques et une détermination constante à renforcer la compétitivité de son économie. L'ambassadeur du Royaume chérifien, Youssef Slaoui (micro) Le Royaume du Maroc a fait de l'intégration africaine, l'un des fondamentaux de sa politique étrangère. A cet égard, il œuvre constamment en faveur de l'établissement d'un partenariat de référence et d'une coopération Sud-Sud mutuellement bénéfique et solidaire au sein de l'Afrique, à laquelle il est intrinsèquement lié par des relations historiques profondes. «Avec le Burkina Faso, nos relations bilatérales sont très excellentes et se caractérisent par une convergence de vues sur les questions d'intérêt commun au niveau des instances régionales, continentales et internationales», a soutenu le Représentant du Royaume chérifien. Une vue des invités au 27e anniversaire de la Fête du Trône Parmi les domaines couverts par la coopération des deux pays basée sur l'échange d'expertise et partage de compétences, il y a notamment la «Défense/Sécurité, la Protection Civile, la Formation Professionnelle, l'Agriculture, le Commerce, la Jeunesse, les Infrastructures Routières, la Sécurité Routière, la Douane, l'Urbanisme et l'Habitat et la Reconnaissance réciproque des permis de conduire nationaux des deux pays», a précisé l’ambassadeur Slaoui. Le ministre des Affaires étrangères, Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré «Notre Agenda bilatéral comprend également l'axe de Coopération Scientifique et Technique. Pour l'année académique 2026/2027, le quota officiel des bourses d'études marocaines est porté au nombre de 250, reparti entre les formations universitaires et professionnelles orientées vers les matières Techniques, d'Ingénieries, la Spécialisation Médicale, les Sciences Juridiques et Economiques, répondant ainsi aux besoins du tissu socio-économique du Burkina Faso, avec un quota spécial dédié aux Pupilles de la Nation», a-t-il également soulevé. Entre le Burkina Faso et le Royaume du Maroc, «l'amitié est une réalité vécue» et «elle se reconnaît dans la constance du dialogue politique, dans la confiance entre nos dirigeants, dans la solidarité entre nos peuples et, surtout, dans les résultats concrets que notre coopération apporte à nos populations», a déclaré le ministre Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré. Photo de famille Le chef de la diplomatie burkinabè a fait savoir que l'année 2025 a marqué une étape importante de la coopération bilatérale car les deux pays ont célébré le soixantième anniversaire de l'établissement de leurs relations diplomatiques, nouées le 21 octobre 1965. Ils ont également tenu, le 10 décembre 2025 à Ouagadougou, la cinquième session de la Commission mixte de coopération. «Cette rencontre n'a pas seulement permis de dresser le bilan du chemin parcouru. Elle a ouvert une nouvelle séquence, avec la signature de douze accords couvrant des domaines essentiels: la protection civile, la sécurité, la formation, l'agriculture, les infrastructures, le commerce, le travail, l'éducation, l'urbanisme et l'habitat, ainsi que le sport et la jeunesse», a souligné le ministre burkinabè en charge des Affaires étrangères, Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré. Une vue large du public Pour lui, leur responsabilité, aujourd'hui est de faire vivre ces engagements. «Un accord ne prend toute sa valeur que lorsqu'il devient une formation accessible, une expertise partagée, une entreprise créée, une infrastructure réalisée, un emploi offert à un jeune ou une amélioration concrète dans la vie de nos concitoyens», a-t-il affirmé, déclarant que c'est à cette diplomatie des résultats que le Burkina Faso veut désormais donner toute sa force. Le ministre burkinabè des Affaires étrangères a tenu également à rendre hommage à l'engagement personnel de l'ambassadeur du Royaume du Maroc au Burkina Faso qui par sa disponibilité, son écoute et son action quotidienne, contribue avec conviction au rapprochement des deux peuples et à la vitalité du partenariat fort qui lie les deux Nations. Par Bernard BOUGOUM L’article 27e Fête du trône: «Avec le Burkina Faso, nos relations bilatérales sont très excellentes» est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: FCT police bust network producing fake diplomatic, govt number plates
items.description: The Federal Capital Territory Police Command has uncovered a criminal network involved in the production and circulation of fake diplomatic and official government number plates allegedly used by criminals to evade security checks and gain access to restricted locations. The Commissioner of Police, Ahmed Sanusi, disclosed this on Friday during a press briefing at the command headquarters in Abuja, saying investigations had exposed both the users of the counterfeit plates and the supply chain behind their production. According to him, the investigation was launched shortly after he assumed office following reports that diplomatic and government registration plates were increasingly being used by unauthorised persons. “Upon my assumption of duty as the Commissioner of Police, FCT Command, my attention was drawn to the proliferation and unauthorized use of diplomatic and official government licence plate numbers by unauthorized individuals. I immediately ordered a comprehensive investigation into this disturbing trend, which revealed that these individuals use such plate numbers as a cover to perpetrate crimes within the Federal Capital Territory and evade detection and arrest,” Sanusi said. The police commissioner said several fake diplomatic and government number plates had been recovered, while suspects linked to the illegal operation were in custody and would be charged to court after investigations. “The suspects from whom these plate numbers were recovered are currently in custody and will be charged to court upon the conclusion of investigation,” he said. Sanusi disclosed that investigators had also identified those producing the counterfeit plates, although they operate outside the FCT. “We are on their trail. We’ve gotten their identities. That’s why we are not displaying our suspects regarding this so that they will not know that we are coming after them,” he added. He revealed that some buyers paid between ₦500,000 and ₦1.7 million to obtain the fake number plates, suggesting the documents were acquired to facilitate criminal activities. “Some of these things are ranging between ₦500,000 to ₦1.7 million for them to procure. This will tell you that they are making such huge expenditure because they have an agenda to fulfil with it,” he said. Sanusi urged residents to report vehicles bearing suspicious diplomatic registration numbers, noting that authentic diplomatic plates follow an established format. “They use these fake numbers to beat security checkpoints. They use them to go into ministries and parastatals unstopped because everybody feels once you are a diplomat or have these plates, you are a big man. Help us identify them. Raise an alarm and we will arrest them,” he said. The commissioner also announced the recovery of stolen public infrastructure during separate intelligence-led operations across several parts of the FCT, including drainage covers, solar-powered street lights, armoured electricity cables and internet communication cables. He described the vandalism of public assets as economic sabotage and warned scrap dealers and other receivers of stolen government property that the command had widened its investigation to dismantle the entire criminal network behind the theft and disposal of public infrastructure. The post FCT police bust network producing fake diplomatic, govt number plates appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ISSER warns Ghana’s gold reserve strategy faces price risks
items.description: The Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER) has cautioned that Ghana’s increasing reliance on gold as part of its international reserves could expose the country to financial risks if global gold prices continue to decline. Speaking at the Post-Revenue Mid-Year Budget Review Forum in Accra, the director of ISSER, Professor Robert Darko Osei, said, “The use of gold for reserves poses some risk given the drop in gold prices on the international market.” He explained that while the Bank of Ghana’s gold accumulation strategy has strengthened the country’s reserve position, fluctuations in international gold prices remain a key vulnerability that policymakers must closely monitor. Professor Osei also argued that the country’s recent success in reducing inflation has come at a significant cost to the central bank. According to him, “The fiscal consolidation and monetary sterilization have helped to contain inflation, but this has come to Bank of Ghana at a very high cost.” He warned that the current policy mix should not become a permanent approach to inflation management. “This approach is certainly not the long-term solution to inflation considering its implications on the Central Bank’s finances,” he stated. Meanwhile, the economist cautioned against pushing inflation excessively below Ghana’s medium-term target, noting that “The medium-term inflation rate is 8 ± 2 percent; efforts to reduce inflation below this optimal rate could have financial and employment implications.” Professor Osei further observed that recent developments on the global energy market present fresh inflationary risks for Ghana. He noted that “The recent increase in oil prices has implications for inflation expectations and prices,” warning that higher fuel costs could reverse some of the gains made in bringing inflation under control. His remarks come as policymakers continue to assess the country’s macroeconomic outlook after the presentation of the Mid-Year Budget Review, with analysts closely watching the sustainability of inflation, reserve management, and broader fiscal reforms.

items.title: Le chocolatier Lindt poursuivi aux États-Unis pour communication trompeuse sur le travail des enfants en Afrique
items.description: Le chocolatier suisse Lindt & Sprüngli devra repondre devant un tribunal federal du district de Columbia d'accusations liees a sa communication sur le travail des enfants dans sa chaîne d'approvisionnement en cacao au Ghana et en Cote d'Ivoire. Selon Bloomberg, le recours a ete depose le 8 mai par International Rights Advocates, une organisation a but non lucratif engagee dans la defense des droits des travailleurs, contre les entites americaines du groupe. L'ONG reproche au fabricant de presenter de maniere trompeuse ses efforts visant a lutter contre le travail des enfants au Ghana et en Cote d'Ivoire, deux de ses principaux pays fournisseurs de cacao. La procedure ne porte pas directement sur les prejudices subis par les enfants, mais se place sous la qualification de la tromperie du consommateur americain, qui se trouve etre le plaignant theorique, dans la mesure ou il a ete induit en erreur par les engagements affiches par Lindt & Sprüngli. En promettant aux consommateurs des produits issus d'un approvisionnement « responsable », Lindt s'expose a une obligation accrue de vigilance et de controle afin de detecter les situations presentant des risques pour les enfants. Les producteurs ivoiriens et ghaneens de cacao ne sont pas parties au litige et la plainte ne prevoit pas, a ce stade, l'indemnisation de victimes identifiees. Elle ne demontre pas davantage une implication directe de Lindt dans l'emploi de mineurs. Les plaignants cherchent principalement a faire cesser des pratiques commerciales jugees trompeuses et a obtenir davantage de transparence dans la chaîne d'approvisionnement du chocolatier. Lindt refute les accusations Le chocolatier suisse juge les accusations « infondees ». Son porte-parole a declare a l'agence de presse suisse AWP que le groupe disposait de « directives relatives aux fournisseurs » et enquetait « systematiquement sur tous les cas suspects de travail des enfants » dans sa chaîne d'approvisionnement. Il a egalement affirme que le groupe prenait la question du travail des mineurs « tres au serieux ». Selon lui, ces accusations ressemblent a des plaintes deja deposees par la meme organisation contre plusieurs autres fabricants de chocolat. En 2025, Lindt & Sprüngli avait annonce son intention de s'approvisionner, a partir de 2026, exclusivement aupres de fournisseurs disposant de systemes de controle et de surveillance du travail des enfants.

items.title: Burkina/Reboisement : Le projet SOLEER met 280 plants en terre à l'université Thomas Sankara
items.description: Le Projet de déploiement du solaire à large échelle et d'électrification rurale (SOLEER), en collaboration avec l'Université Thomas Sankara, a organisé, le jeudi 30 juillet 2026, une journée de reboisement compensatoire sur le site de l'université. Cette initiative s'inscrit dans le cadre des travaux de renforcement du système de télécommunications du réseau national interconnecté de la SONABEL. Au total, 280 plants ont été mis en terre sur une superficie d'un hectare. Étudiants, responsables du projet SOLEER et autorités universitaires se sont fortement mobilisés pour assurer le succès de cette opération, qui vise à contribuer à la restauration du couvert végétal et à la préservation de l'environnement. Le président de l'université Thomas Sankara, le Pr Didier Zoungrana, a salué le choix porté sur son institution pour accueillir cette activité de reboisement. Il a exprimé sa gratitude aux responsables du projet SOLEER ainsi qu'au ministère en charge de l'Énergie pour cette initiative. Le président de l'université Thomas Sankara Pr Didier Zoungrana en train d'ajouter du sable dans le trou après avoir fini de planter son arbre « Vous avez fait le bon choix. Car nous faisons de la protection de l'environnement et du verdissement notre credo, à l'image de notre père de la Révolution, Thomas Sankara. Planter un arbre est un acte simple, mais de sens immense. C'est un legs que nous faisons aujourd'hui au profit des générations futures. C'est un engagement que nous prenons envers notre planète et une contribution concrète à la lutte contre les effets néfastes des changements climatiques », a souligné le président de l'université Thomas Sankara. Pour lui, en accueillant ce reboisement, l'université confirme sa vocation d'institution engagée pour le développement durable tout en se dotant d'un cadre paysager propice aux études et à la recherche. Il a rassuré que ce bosquet aura un entretien adéquat grâce à l'ensemble du personnel universitaire et des étudiants. « Planter un arbre est un acte louable, mais l'entretenir reste un défi. Nous prenons l'engagement de relever ce défi », a-t-il terminé. Le président de l'université Thomas Sankara Selon le représentant du ministre en charge de l'Énergie, Jean-Baptiste Kaboré, le reboisement compensatoire constitue une mesure concrète permettant d'atténuer les impacts environnementaux liés à la réalisation des infrastructures. « Au-delà du respect des exigences réglementaires, il traduit notre volonté de restaurer les écosystèmes, d'améliorer les paysages, de renforcer les puits de carbone et de transmettre aux générations futures un environnement plus sain », a-t-il indiqué. Le représentant du ministre en charge de l'Energie, Jean-Baptiste Kaboré Et d'ajouter : « Les défis climatiques auxquels notre pays est confronté nous imposent de développer des solutions intégrées. Nous devons produire davantage d'énergie propre tout en protégeant nos ressources forestières. Nous devons accélérer l'accès universel à l'électricité tout en réduisant notre empreinte environnementale. Nous devons bâtir une économie plus compétitive tout en préservant les bases naturelles de notre développement. C'est cette vision que traduit la stratégie énergétique du gouvernement ». Le représentant du ministre souhaite que cette initiative inspire d'autres projets publics et privés. Afin que chaque investissement contribue simultanément au développement économique, à la création d'emplois, à la protection de l'environnement et à l'amélioration des conditions de vie de nos populations. La photo de famille « Le reboisement compensatoire que nous lançons aujourd'hui traduit concrètement cet engagement et s'inscrit dans la dynamique de réduire les émissions de gaz à effet de serre de 318 000 (CO2/an) comme s'est fixé le projet SOLEER. Il faut rappeler que le projet SOLEER, à terme, devrait raccorder 120 000 ménages à travers 300 nouvelles localités électrifiées, renforcer le réseau national interconnecté, accroître la production d'énergie par la réalisation de centrales solaires photovoltaïques de 325 MWc et impacter 700 000 bénéficiaires d'un service d'électricité nouveau ou amélioré, dont 350 000 femmes », a fait savoir le représentant du coordonnateur du projet SOLEER, Teeg Wendé Aymar Kaboré. Le représentant du coordonnateur du projet SOLEER, Teeg Wendé Aymar Kaboré Pour lui, chaque arbre planté ce jour représente un engagement en faveur de la lutte contre la désertification, de la séquestration du carbone, de l'amélioration de la qualité de l'air et de la conservation de la biodiversité. Selon lui, chaque arbre planté constitue un symbole de leur volonté de concilier développement économique, l'accès à l'énergie et la protection de l'environnement. Il a toutefois rappelé que la réussite de cette initiative dépendra de la capacité de l'université à assurer l'entretien des plantes. « Notre ambition est que ces arbres deviennent, dans quelques années, une véritable forêt universitaire, offrant de l'ombre, améliorant le microclimat du campus, favorisant la biodiversité et rappelant aux générations futures que le développement durable repose sur des actions concrètes et responsables », a notifié M. Kaboré. À travers cette opération de reboisement compensatoire, le projet SOLEER entend concilier le développement des infrastructures énergétiques et de télécommunications avec la préservation de l'environnement Rama Diallo Lefaso.net

items.title: PPP's Central Executive Committee to deliberate creation of new administrative units: secretary general
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The PPP’s Central Executive Committee (CEC) will deliberate on the matter of creating new administrative units, which should be created through the mechanism provided in the Constitution and by means of an executive order, the party’s secretary general Nayyar Bokhari said on Friday. “The Constitution of Pakistan has clearly laid down the complete procedure. Without a two-thirds majority in the relevant provincial assembly, the National Assembly and the Senate, neither the creation of new provinces nor any alteration in provincial boundaries is possible,” he said while speaking to Dawn . “New provinces cannot be created through an executive order. They can only be created through a constitutional decision of Parliament,” he added. Bokhari’s statement comes a day after Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi echoed demands by multiple political parties for more provinces or administrative units. Those advocating for more administrative units view them as a way to improve governance. The PPP, which is the ruling party in Sindh, has opposed the creation of any new administrative units in the province but has advocated for the creation of a South Punjab province. Discussing the matter during his conversation with Dawn , Bokhari said, “If there is genuine seriousness about establishing new provinces, including South Punjab, the matter should be brought before Parliament and the constitutional requirements should be fulfilled.” He called upon Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who belongs to the ruling party in Punjab as well as at the Centre, to initiate the process of creating more administrative units from his own province. The PPP secretary general also recalled that a resolution for the creation of a South Punjab province was pending in the Punjab Assembly. Bokhari said federal ministers should raise the matter of creating new administrative units in the federal cabinet and, after obtaining its approval, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif should consult PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on this “important national issue”. He added that the PPP’s CEC would deliberate on the matter and “every decision will be taken with due regard to the Constitution, democracy and the will of the people”. In the recent past, the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) — an ally of the PML-N-led ruling coalition — has repeatedly demanded that Karachi be designated a province separate from Sindh. However, the PPP, which rules Sindh and is also an ally of the PML-N government at the Centre along with MQM-P, has strongly opposed the suggested move. On the other hand, the PPP and the PTI have long advocated for a South Punjab province. President of the Istehkam Pakistan Party (IPP) and Federal Communications Minister Abdul Aleem Khan had urged political parties to accept the need for smaller provinces, demanding that each of the four provinces be divided into four provinces each for a total of 16. He said this was an immediate and sustainable solution to the problems of people living in far-flung areas. Addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 being held in Islamabad on Thursday, Interior Minister Naqvi said there was “only one solution” to improving the country’s overall condition: “You will have to take [the matter of] administrative units, provinces or whatever you may call it, to the public.” He added, “All political parties should sit together in a single room, whether for a day, a month or a year. They will have to settle every issue of their country, including new units and provinces.” “The system we are living under has collapsed. Problems cannot be solved through it,” he said. “If this system continues, we will still be sitting here 10 years from now discussing the same issues.” He noted that only structural change could break the cycle and that a reset was necessary, while adding that Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts , even while being hailed globally, were “simply firefighting”. Responding to Naqvi’s statement, Bokhari said that if there were flaws in the system, the appropriate forum to address them was Parliament, not the media. “Who should be held responsible if the system is not functioning properly?” asked the PPP leader. He said the country’s recent diplomatic successes were an asset for the entire nation, with Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir playing a key role in these successes. The PPP leader added that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, and the interior minister had also fulfilled their respective responsibilities, adding that it was now the federal government’s responsibility to translate these diplomatic achievements into economic stability and public relief. “If the economy does not improve, responsibility will rest with the federal government,” he declared.

items.title: Fête du Trône : affluence record au Festival des Plages Maroc Telecom à M'diq
items.description: Plus de 670.000 festivaliers ont participé aux deux grandes soirées organisées à M'diq à l'occasion des célébrations de la glorieuse Fête du Trône, dans le cadre de la 22è édition du Festival des Plages Maroc Telecom. Une mobilisation exceptionnelle qui confirme le succès populaire de cet événement culturel majeur. À l'occasion des festivités célébrant la glorieuse Fête du Trône, le 22è Festival des Plages Maroc Telecom a connu une affluence exceptionnelle lors des deux grandes soirées organisées à M'diq. Le mercredi 29 juillet, la soirée animée par la star de la chanson arabe Ragheb Alama, aux côtés d'Ihssane Ragragui, a rassemblé près de 320.000 festivaliers, venus vivre un moment de fête, de partage et de communion autour de la musique. Le jeudi 30 juillet, la ferveur populaire s'est encore intensifiée avec près de 350.000 festivaliers réunis pour les prestations très attendues du groupe Fnaire et de Douzi, dans une ambiance festive et conviviale. Ces deux soirées, marquées par une mobilisation exceptionnelle du public, illustrent le succès de cette 22è édition du Festival des Plages Maroc Telecom et confirment son statut de rendez-vous culturel incontournable de l'été au Maroc. Retour en images sur ces deux soirées d'exception placées sous le signe de la glorieuse Fête du Trône. Pour rappel, le Festival des Plages Maroc Telecom se poursuit jusqu'au 21 août 2026 à travers M'diq, Tanger, Al Hoceima et Saïdia, avec une programmation artistique riche et variée. items.title: Climate Change Is Destabilizing the Ground Beneath Our Feet
items.description: On geologic timescales, the Earth is a dynamic place. Tectonic plates shift. Continents move. Mountains rise and fall. But during humanity’s tenure on Earth, the ground beneath our feet has largely stayed put. That stable period may now be at an end. Climate change began in the atmosphere, where greenhouse gases accumulate, trapping heat from the sun. The planet’s waters reacted—precipitation patterns shifted, glaciers and ice caps began melting, the ocean generously sponged up heat and carbon dioxide. When the Earth’s waters shift, so does solid ground. Now warming is destabilizing land across the planet, and geology is becoming a real-time science. In more and more places, the floor is giving way. In Alaska, Norway, Greenland, Chile, and New Zealand, as well as across the European Alps, mountains are crumbling. As glaciers retreat, some at unprecedented rates, they leave behind unstable cliffs that were once supported by ice. In 2023, one collapsed into a fjord in Greenland and generated a 660-foot wave that sent ripples through the Earth detected on monitoring stations worldwide for nine days. In Alaska last year, a landslide-generated tsunami struck in a fjord frequented by cruise ships. In Switzerland the same year, part of a mountain glacier detached entirely, burying the village of Blatten in a cataclysmic landslide. In the past decade or so, scientists have collected enough dramatic examples of this phenomenon to suggest that they’re clearly not isolated incidents, but part of a pattern linking the loss of glaciers with landslide risk. And those landslides could get larger. When the glaciers melted after the last glacial maximum, about 20,000 years ago, the landslides that followed were orders of magnitude larger than any we’ve seen in recorded history. But because some of today’s glaciers have persisted in the landscape longer than those of that glacial period did, they’ve had time to carve steep, unstable cliffs. This means that “we haven’t seen the upper bounds of landslides yet,” Kristian Svennevig, a geologist at the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland, told me. In Arctic regions in the near future, the magnitude of landslides could exceed any scientists know of in the geologic record. Along with glaciers, permafrost holds mountains together at high altitudes and latitudes worldwide. It, too, is in retreat, as scientists predicted in the 1980s and as has now become apparent across the Arctic reaches. In the Brooks Range, home of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, long-frozen mountains have started to spontaneously deform and collapse within the past few decades or so, as their permafrost glue gives way. “We’re pushing these mountains into a state of disequilibrium, where they need to adjust their slopes in order to match the climate of today,” the independent Alaskan geologist Bretwood Higman told me. They’re essentially too steep for this warmer temperature regime. “As a geologist, I’ve found it shocking how widespread the sudden increase in landslide activity is,” Higman said. When you’re used to thinking on scales that span tens of thousands of years, to see these changes play out over human lifetimes—“it’s very dramatic.” The thawing of permafrost in mountainous regions already threatens infrastructure. Denali National Park is close to finishing a $100 million bridge that will span a moving permafrost landslide. In the Brooks Range, engineers are pumping refrigerant underground to refreeze permafrost and stabilize pipelines. And mountains aren’t the only land giving way. Cement-solid Arctic ground is turning into bogs. Communities across Alaska have had to relocate as their homes, fuel tanks, sewage lagoons, and garbage dumps tip, spill, or sink. Elsewhere, as massive underground chunks of ancient ice melt, the surrounding earth collapses into the voids left behind, buckling roads and swallowing buildings. In Siberia, once-trapped methane explodes from under permafrost to cause 100-foot craters. “When permafrost thaws, it changes everything,” Sue Natali, an Arctic-climate scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, told me. Natali and her colleagues are seeing the thaw speed up too. “That is not a maybe thing, and it is not a local thing. It is a pan-Arctic thing,” she said. Climate is also shifting the land at lower latitudes. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, which means more frequent and extreme rainfall events. In recent years, scientists have begun modeling how this kind of rain will increase landslide risk , and linking individual events to storms made more dramatic by climate change. “Harder, more intense, longer-duration rainfall has a greater possibility to generate landslides,” Jonathan Godt, who leads the United States Geological Survey’s landslide-hazards program, told me. These kind of debris flows and mudslides now threaten more communities. In North Carolina, Hurricane Helene triggered more than 2,000 landslides in a week. In California, slopes wiped clean by logging and drought-fueled wildfires slough away after heavy rain—one mudslide in Montecito destroyed 100 homes and killed 23 people in 2018. Landslides already cause $20 billion in damage globally, and that cost will only climb with climate change. Already, scientists have been able to catalog the effects of melting glaciers, thawing permafrost, and extreme rain. Other dramatic consequences of shifting precipitation patterns—volcanic eruptions and earthquakes—are only just coming into focus. More than a decade ago, in his book Waking the Giant , the University College London volcanologist Bill McGuire compiled decades of paleoclimate research to predict that climate change could lead to more volcanic eruptions and earthquakes. An increase in volcanic and tectonic activity would be a natural response to the end of a glacial period. For thousands of years now, the Earth’s crust, which was weighted down by ice, has been slowly bouncing back. That process releases pressure from long-subdued faults and volcanoes, such as those in Iceland. Human-caused climate change is only accelerating these processes. And water, whether from extreme rainfall or glacial melt, can percolate in cracks underground to increase pressure on rock and reduce friction along faults, triggering both earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Last year, researchers in Switzerland and France found some of the clearest evidence so far that glacial melt could indeed be affecting seismic hazards in high-altitude regions. After a period of intense glacial melt in 2015, a series of small quakes struck the Grandes Jorasses on Mont Blanc Massif, on the border of France and Italy; the probability of a 3.0-magnitude earthquake rose by 10 times, Toni Kraft, a seismologist at the Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich and one of the authors of a related paper, told me. These quakes are still small, but they could trigger rockfall events that are already on the rise across the Alps. Falk Amelung, a geoscientist at the University of Miami, has also argued—somewhat controversially—that climate-driven extreme rainfall might have led to the dramatic 2018 eruption of Hawaii’s Kīlauea volcano. Scientists have not been able to find an obvious triggering mechanism for the eruption, and Amelung hypothesized that rainfall had infiltrated the volcano’s edifice and increased pore pressure in the rock, kilometers down, to the highest rates in almost 50 years. USGS volcanologists were unconvinced : A link between heavy precipitation and some types of volcanic activity is widely accepted, but some scientists still reject the theory that an eruption such as Kīlauea’s could be caused by water reaching the magma below. If Amelung and others in his camp are right, though, as many as 700 volcanoes could be at risk of dome explosions and flank collapse over the next 80 years, he calculated. “The system must be heavily stressed in a way that it’s close to breaking anyway,” he told me. “And then this small stress change due to water brings it over the edge.” During Earth’s long history, small perturbations have caused millennia-long swings between hothouse and icehouse conditions. The amount of carbon dioxide that we have pumped into the atmosphere, at a higher rate than ever before in Earth’s geologic history, is a pretty significant perturbation, which then causes its own significant perturbations. “The crust is not isolated. It’s always connected. The climate, the fluid layers, the solid layer—you cannot separate them,” Benedikt Soja, a geoscientist at ETH Zurich, told me. The atmosphere, ocean, and land are interacting systems, and their fragile equilibrium is reacting together to the stress we’ve put on them.

items.title: ‘South East no longer marginalised’ – Information minister Idris
items.description: By Steve Oko Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, has said the South-East is no longer marginalised but now enjoys a greater sense of belonging in the affairs of the country. Idris made the assertion on Friday while responding to questions during a press conference in Umuahia, Abia State, on the heels of the maiden South East regional security summit held on Thursday in the capital city. He urged Ndigbo to discard the belief that they are being sidelined, arguing that even if such perceptions existed in the past, they no longer apply under the administration of President Bola Tinubu. He cited ongoing road and infrastructure projects across the zone, as well as the appointment of former Ebonyi State Governor, Senator Dave Umahi, to the strategic position of Minister of Works, as evidence that the South-East is no longer being relegated. When confronted with claims that insecurity in the South-East is linked to the continued detention of Nnamdi Kanu and the Federal Government’s refusal to engage Biafra agitators in dialogue to address their grievances—while repentant terrorists in the North are being granted pardon—the minister declined to comment, saying Kanu’s matter is already before the court. He, however, maintained that President Tinubu is committed to inclusivity and addressing injustice and every form of exclusion that may have existed in the past. Idris reaffirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to restoring lasting peace and security in the South-East, declaring that President Bola Tinubu’s administration is determined to create an environment where businesses, industries and communities in the region can thrive. The minister, who spoke on the heels of the inaugural South-East Regional Security Summit on Thursday, said the Tinubu administration recognised the enormous economic potential of the South-East and is implementing security and economic reforms aimed at unlocking that potential. According to him, the Federal Government believes that sustainable security goes beyond military operations and must be driven by economic opportunities, infrastructure development, youth empowerment and active community participation. “The message from the Federal Government is clear: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration is committed to ensuring that every Nigerian, in every part of the country, has the right to live, work and pursue prosperity in a safe and secure environment,” the minister said. He described the South-East Security Summit, organised by the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Community Engagement (South-East) in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Defence and hosted by the Abia State Government, as a critical platform for charting lasting solutions to insecurity in the region. The minister commended the organisers and participants, noting that the large turnout reflected a shared understanding that security is a collective responsibility involving government, security agencies, traditional rulers, community leaders and citizens. Idris said the Federal Government has continued to strengthen Nigeria’s security architecture through enhanced support for security agencies, improved intelligence gathering, greater operational capacity and stronger collaboration among federal, state and community stakeholders. He stressed that lasting peace could not be achieved through force alone. “Peace and stability are strengthened when citizens have economic opportunities, young people have hope, businesses can thrive and communities have confidence in government,” he stated. The minister explained that the Renewed Hope Agenda situates security within a broader framework of economic development, infrastructure renewal, human capital investment and social inclusion. He also defended the economic reforms introduced by the Tinubu administration, saying they were necessary to address deep-rooted structural challenges inherited by the government. According to him, the administration inherited fiscal pressures, declining revenues, exchange rate distortions and other structural weaknesses that had hampered Nigeria’s economic growth for years. He said the removal of fuel subsidy and reforms in the foreign exchange market were designed to create a more transparent, productive and investment-friendly economy capable of delivering long-term prosperity. Idris acknowledged that the reforms had imposed short-term hardships on Nigerians but noted that the government had rolled out interventions, including support for small businesses, consumer credit schemes, student loans and social protection programmes to cushion the impact. He maintained that a peaceful South-East would naturally attract greater investment, stimulate economic growth and create jobs for the people. “A peaceful South-East will attract investment. A growing economy will create opportunities. An empowered population will strengthen national stability,” he said. The minister reiterated President Tinubu’s commitment to building an inclusive Nigeria where every region has the opportunity to realise its full economic potential and every citizen can look forward to a more prosperous future. He also urged journalists to eschew misinformation, sensational and fake news, and always endeavour to report responsibly for peace to thrive in society. The minister was flanked at the press conference by the Commissioner for Information in Abia State, Prince Okey Kanu; and the National President of the Radio, Television, Theatre and Arts Workers Union of Nigeria (RATTAWU), Prince Emeka Kalu (Magic Fingers). The post ‘South East no longer marginalised’ – Information minister Idris appeared first on Vanguard News .
